title: Do chemically active droplets hollow into self-made liquid shells from noise, and does a shell's lumen hold a cargo better than a slow-diffusion twin?
summary: Bauermann, Bartolucci, Boekhoven, Weber & Jülicher (arXiv:2306.10852) and Bergmann et al. (Nat Commun 14, 6552, 2023) show that when an active droplet makes its material outside and degrades it inside, the core falls below the spinodal and hollows into a stable liquid shell. Many shells coexist, Ostwald ripening is suppressed, and large growing shells fold and split. The active-emulsion class has no hollow bodies, and the ledger's only self-made wall around cargo (the FCH shell) failed its slow-D twin. This is a second, non-amphiphile route to a wall, in a class that already swims and divides.

Corrected summary: Bauermann, Bartolucci, Boekhoven, Weber & Jülicher (Phys. Rev. Research 5, 043246, 2023; arXiv:2306.10852) show the following in a binary Cahn-Hilliard model with piecewise-linear turnover. When the dense-phase turnover is raised, the droplet core falls below the spinodal and hollows into a stable liquid shell. In emulsions seeded with random droplets and shells, many shells coexist and Ostwald ripening is suppressed. Growing shells in an unbounded system go through an l = 2 shape instability, fold and split. Bergmann et al. (Nat Commun 14, 6552, 2023) confirm the mechanism experimentally in fueled coacervates. Activation happens mostly outside the droplet and deactivation inside, which depletes the core and leaves a stationary shell. Their model predicts that droplets and shells can coexist, but each microreactor showed only one object. Whether shells form from a uniform noisy start is untested in either paper. Fig. 1 uses equal mobilities; D_dil > D_den is suggested in the text as making shells easier. Citation check: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10582082/ partly: Opened.
